A bit about me

I just wrapped up a Bachelor of Engineering in Electronic Systems at Conestoga College. Somewhere between my second and third year I realized I liked the projects where I had to touch every layer, not just one, and I've been chasing that feeling since. Two co-op terms at Velatron Technologies working on industrial test fixtures, safety interlock systems, and control hardware. Three complete embedded builds on my own time, each one bigger than the last.

The parts of engineering I care about the most are the ones that show up when things go sideways. Whether a sensor actually catches the failure case. Whether the enclosure survives five redesigns. Whether the system recovers on its own or needs a person standing next to it with a debugger. That's what the projects below are about.

Right now I'm in Kitchener, planning a move to the Greater Vancouver area. I'm most interested in embedded firmware, hardware design, and test engineering roles where I can keep building things that get turned on and used.

PortaPill, an automated pill dispenser

Capstone II / January to August 2026 / with Blaise Swan

A three-compartment automated pill dispenser built around a specific reliability question. How do you actually confirm a dose was delivered, and not just commanded?

Control is split across two microcontrollers. An RP2350 (Raspberry Pi Pico 2) runs real-time motor control, scheduling, and delivery sensing. An ESP32-S3 handles the touchscreen UI, Wi-Fi, and a web dashboard hosted directly on the device so caretakers can check status from a phone browser without any cloud service in the loop.

Every dispense is verified two independent ways. An IR beam-break sensor catches pill transit through the chute, a piezoelectric sensor picks up impact in the collection drawer, and a Hall-effect sensor confirms the drawer was opened for pickup. If verification fails, the system retries automatically before reporting a persistent fault.

Networked elevator control system

Engineering Projects VI / Spring 2025 / with Kyle Dick

A distributed elevator control system that emulates real industrial automation practice. A Raspberry Pi reads floor requests from a MySQL-backed web GUI and sends commands over CAN bus to an Arduino-driven motor controller. Every event is logged twice, once at the application layer and once on the CAN network itself, for full traceability.

The feature I'm most proud of is Maintenance Mode. Dedicated STM32 boards give technicians physical, network-independent control of the elevator for on-site servicing. If the GUI or network goes down, the elevator can still be operated safely from the hardware itself.

  • TimingGetting the GUI, PHP backend, and C++ controller to agree on state was harder than it sounds. Small mismatches caused skipped or repeated floor commands until we tightened up the polling and acknowledgment logic.
  • AudioReal-time two-way emergency voice over ALSA and TCP sockets had jitter and first-connect bugs that took a few evenings of packet-poking to nail down.
  • Mode separationKeeping Standard, Sabbath, and Maintenance modes cleanly separated while still logging every transition meant rewriting the state machine twice before I was happy with it.

First co-op term

Electrical / Electronic Engineering Technician January to April 2025

Landed in the transformer and inductor test lab. Spent most of the term on hands-on component characterization for production quality control.

What I actually did
  • Built custom test fixtures for transformer, inductor, and coil components, then used Voltech equipment to measure resistance, inductance, and capacitance across windings to determine pass or fail against manufacturing specs
  • Ran components in an isolated environment under controlled temperature and humidity to verify electrical characteristics held across operating ranges
  • Troubleshot failed components on the line, repaired what I could, escalated to manufacturing specialists when needed, and scrapped parts that could not be saved
  • Took on an open-ended R&D project to introduce a vector network analyzer for magnetic core characterization, expanding the lab's testing capability

Second co-op term

Electrical / Electronic Engineering Technician September to December 2025 · returned by request

Invited back for a second term, this time with more design ownership. Moved from test to actual control-system design work on production machinery.

What I actually did
  • Designed and built a mode-verification and safety interlock system for an industrial rolling machine, using visual indicators to show operators which mode they are in and locking out the machine if they try to run it in the wrong state
  • Designed a control box for heavy-industry winding equipment running on high AC wall voltage, working from schematic through fabrication alongside senior engineers
  • Modelled fixture components in SolidWorks, manufactured them via 3D printing, and maintained BOMs throughout the design cycle for production-line test stations
  • Authored operational procedure documents and instructional manuals for production machinery, coordinating with senior engineers to verify accuracy before release to the floor
